title: ‘Smart’ Implants Are Driving Up Health Costs — Even When Patients Don’t Ask for Them
summary: Two patients are suing after allegedly waking from knee replacement surgery and learning they’d received “smart” joints, capable of transmitting data. Researchers say their usefulness is unproven, yet Medicare and private insurers pay doctors to monitor such devices.
content: Steve Russak, 70, of Santa Rosa Valley, California, woke up from knee replacement surgery last year to a text message. It was from the company that made his new knee. Over the next few days, the company, Zimmer Biomet, texted four times. Russak didn’t understand the inquiries asking him to use an app, he said. Finally, a company representative called and offered help setting up some accessories, Russak told KFF Health News. “I said, ‘What? I don’t know what you’re talking about.’” It turned out Russak did not receive just any old replacement of bone and cartilage. He’d had a “smart knee” put in — an artificial joint called the Persona IQ with a lithium-ion battery, sensors, and transmitter that, should he authorize it, would send data about his gait and range of motion to his clinicians and Zimmer. Russak is suing the doctor, Zimmer, and Canary Medical, a health technology company that helped develop the device. In his lawsuit , Russak claims the knee was an “unauthorized implantation” and that, according to Zimmer’s “patient-facing materials,” he should have been given the option to opt out of data collection or decline the knee altogether, but wasn’t. Russak said he doesn’t want to set up the device to collect and transmit data for several reasons, including his privacy. Now that it’s in his body, though, he said it poses potential disruptions. For example, Russak said he recently couldn’t get an MRI because of compatibility issues. Neither the doctor nor the doctor’s lawyer responded to multiple requests for comment. The case is ongoing, with the next hearing scheduled for December. Russak said he has dropped the fraud and breach of fiduciary duty allegations originally filed against the doctor but is continuing to sue on other grounds, including lack of informed consent. The doctor has yet to respond to the complaint in court. Both Zimmer and Canary filed initial responses denying “each and every allegation” in Russak’s complaint. They have offered a variety of defenses, including that any damages are the fault of another party or, as Zimmer’s response said, caused by actions or reactions “not reasonably foreseeable.” Canary Medical did not respond to requests for comment. Zimmer spokesperson Troy Kirkpatrick declined to comment on lawsuits against the company but said that “nearly 90%” of surveyed patients who received Zimmer’s joint replacements report they would choose an orthopedic device with remote monitoring capabilities again in the future. “The transmission of post-operative recovery data requires patient authorization at the time the patient sets up an account and is designed to support patient-surgeon relationships and postoperative care,” Kirkpatrick said in an emailed statement. He added that Zimmer takes privacy and compliance with regulations “very seriously.” Steve Russak says he didn’t understand the text messages he received after knee replacement surgery asking him to use an app. He later learned he’d had a smart knee put in, he says. (Hannah Norman/KFF Health News) The smart knee is part of a burgeoning trend in American medicine. While Zimmer introduced its device as “ the world’s first and only ” FDA-approved smart knee in 2021, there’s now a range of internet-connected devices — from implants to external products such as blood pressure monitors — that report data about patients’ conditions to doctors or other medical professionals. To proponents, the products offer the chance for better care: They can provide measurements showing whether a patient’s glucose is swerving out of control, for instance. However, enhanced monitoring comes with potential drawbacks, including threats to privacy, and some doctors and researchers caution there is little evidence that smart devices improve health outcomes. There’s “a lot of enthusiasm for remote monitoring technologies. There is tremendous potential,” said Sanket Dhruva, a University of California-San Francisco cardiologist and digital health researcher. But there’s a need for more rigorous data, he said. “We’re getting all this data — is this helping our patients recover better? That’s what we really care about.” Nonetheless, such devices generally mean more money for doctors, who can charge to examine the information they collect. Monitoring Every Step Both Medicare and private insurers reimburse clinical professionals for reviewing data from smart devices. In 2024, nearly 1 million Medicare beneficiaries received that service, known as “remote patient monitoring,” according to the Department of Health and Human Services’ Office of Inspector General. Medicare, the federal program covering older Americans and some with disabilities, paid medical providers $536 million for remote monitoring, more than double what it paid three years earlier. A review by the Peterson-KFF Health System Tracker found about 300,000 adults with employer-sponsored insurance received at least one remote monitoring claim in 2023. Medicare has proposed pulling back on some reimbursements after the department’s inspector general warned remote monitoring poses fraud risks: About 43% of patients in 2024 didn’t receive the full suite of services defined by the program — which includes educating the patient about the device and monitoring data for changes in health. The watchdog also cautioned that companies sometimes cold-call patients to offer and sign them up for devices they may not need. The internet-connected devices may also pose risks to privacy or expose patients to unexpected consequences. In 2018, ProPublica reported that insurers watched the performance of CPAP machines and, determining some patients weren’t using them, denied coverage for replacement supplies such as masks. In the case of Zimmer, Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services spokesperson Christopher Krepich emailed KFF Health News that “CMS payment does not mean the agency endorses a manufacturer’s marketing claims or guarantees that a technology improves outcomes for every patient.” He said the agency regularly evaluates its reimbursement policies. Russak’s Medicare account shows the program paid for his surgery and knee implant, but it has not received any claims related to remote monitoring for the device, which he has not set up to transmit data. The smart knee is one of the flagship orthopedic products of Indiana-based Zimmer Biomet, which also manufactures non-connected knee joints. The company — which hired professional strongman, actor, and former California governor Arnold Schwarzenegger to pitch its products as its “chief movement officer” — sold some $3.3 billion in knee joints last year. Russak’s Medicare account shows the program paid for his surgery and knee implant, but it has not received any claims related to remote monitoring for the device, which he has not set up to transmit data. (Hannah Norman/KFF Health News) Up the California coast in Contra Costa County, Jodi Murphy filed a lawsuit against Zimmer, Canary Medical, and her doctor after receiving a Persona IQ knee implant and being registered to use Zimmer’s app. The lawsuit alleges the doctor and companies were at fault because they acted “without disclosing this device or obtaining Plaintiff’s specific informed consent for its use.” The doctor and her practice denied all allegations . Zimmer’s attorneys have said the company “does not practice medicine and as a matter of law had no duty to obtain consent to the treatment provided by her physician.” A hearing is scheduled for February. The doctor did not respond to requests for comment. Murphy and her lawyer declined to comment. Russak’s lawsuit alleges his doctor told him he “had not disclosed the electronic nature, wireless transmission functions, or data-collection capabilities of the Persona IQ to prior patients in whom he had implanted the same device.” It goes on to cite that exchange as evidence that the companies “failed to adequately educate” the doctor. “I don’t believe that Zimmer or Canary are training the doctors, and it’s an issue,” Russak told KFF Health News. Zimmer’s website says the implant allows care teams to “monitor and personalize” a patient’s experience and improve a practice’s efficiency. Many patients prefer the remote option, the company’s literature says. Farther down the webpage, the company says the implant is “not intended to support clinical decision-making” and has “not been shown to provide any clinical benefit.” The company also mentions the potential financial rewards for surgeons who implant the device — including ongoing payments for remote monitoring. ‘Nice-To-Have’ vs. ‘Need-To-Have’ Kevin Bozic, an orthopedic surgeon who is chair of surgery and perioperative care at the University of Texas-Austin, reviewed research on the Zimmer smart knee provided by Zimmer spokesperson Kirkpatrick at KFF Health News’ request. “None of them compare Persona IQ to a more conventional [knee] implant,” he wrote in an email. Bozic said orthopedic surgeons he knows are “ambivalent” about Zimmer’s smart knee devices and many don’t use them. The implant is the “most generic part of the operation and really doesn’t have a big impact at all on the outcome.” In theory, he said, the data collected by the device about the number of steps a patient takes and the joint’s range of motion makes for better care. If a patient becomes more sedentary, that could be a useful signal for clinicians, he said. But, in practice, “it’s a nice-to-have, certainly not a need-to-have,” Bozic said, “certainly not something that I would want to add significant cost to the procedure for.” Surgeons already check on patients and ask to be informed if their health changes, he said. “It’s overkill to have it in the knee.” Smart-knee manufacturers have also profited from a different Medicare benefit — a “new technology add-on payment” — that effectively temporarily subsidizes the adoption of otherwise money-losing new devices, thereby encouraging innovation. (The extra payment for Persona IQ lapsed in fall 2024.) The payment program has undergone several adjustments in recent years. Beginning in late 2020 — until the government adjusted the benefit this year — there was no requirement that new technology substantially improve on older devices or pills. That lack of a requirement, predictably, meant more qualifying therapies. A 2025 study found an average of four approved annually in the near decade before the 2020 change; in the next four fiscal years, the authors said, the average moved up to nearly 15 a year. The subsidy has lasting benefits for the manufacturers, said Dhruva, the UCSF cardiologist, who studies digital technologies and reimbursement. Medicare’s reimbursements are based on the average costs of a procedure. Since the subsidy increases the cost of the procedure, it increases the average costs, too — thereby driving up the basis for future costs. Indeed, Dhruva said, the problem of payments for unproven services is present in Medicare reimbursement for remote patient monitoring, too. Dhruva said there is a dearth of evidence showing the value of remote monitoring generally and of smart knees in particular, though taxpayers have been subsidizing it. “In general, the field is in need of much more rigorous data.” Then there are the privacy concerns — the implications of what happens when someone the patient doesn’t want to get the data does. Overall, these devices are dealing with “quite a bit of data, and oftentimes the issue really crystallizes around patients’ not understanding the information collection, use, and disclosure,” said Kate Black, a health data privacy lawyer not involved with the Russak or Murphy cases. Consent standards for devices such as a smart knee “should be quite high,” she said, because, unlike a wearable product, an implanted device stays in for years. “Every step you take, they know every step you take,” Russak said. title: ‘Medicare for All’ Is Back on Drawing Board. Does It Stand a Better Chance This Time?
summary: Some incoming lawmakers told voters they’d fight for universal, government-funded health coverage. Julie Rovner, KFF Health News’ chief Washington correspondent, writes about what the coming health debate has in common with past fights — and something that’s different this time around.
content: History doesn’t repeat itself, but it does rhyme, as the saying goes. That’s certainly true of the coming fight over “Medicare for All.” The midterm elections saw victories by several candidates who made universal, government-funded health coverage, or some variation thereof, a central pillar of their campaigns, including new Democratic U.S. senators-elect from Michigan, Maine, Iowa, and Texas. They — and many of their soon-to-be colleagues — say they will push the new Democratic majorities in the House and Senate to finally solve the healthcare affordability problem, which so many voters complained about on the campaign trail. But while virtually every elected official supports making healthcare available and affordable for all Americans, the details of getting there have cleaved the Democratic Party the last several times healthcare topped the national agenda. The Clinton health reform effort in 1993-94 fractured over differences within the Democratic majority, as those who wanted a dramatic overhaul like Medicare for All argued with those who saw incremental changes — such as a public option — as more politically feasible. The Affordable Care Act — which, despite incendiary politics, made incremental reforms — barely squeaked into law after similar disputes in 2009. And, so far, it appears history is about to write another stanza of this epic poem. ‘It’s Cosplay’ So why is something so popular in the abstract so hard to accomplish? For one thing, most Americans have no real idea what the phrase “Medicare for All” actually means. “It’s cosplay,” said Nicholas Bagley, a law professor at the University of Michigan who has written about health policy for years. “When you say ‘Medicare for All,’ people think ‘Healthcare — good. We should have more of it.’” Mollyann Brodie — who oversees KFF’s public opinion and survey research program as executive vice president and chief operating officer of the health information nonprofit — points out that in the long history of Medicare for All, support rises and falls dramatically depending on how the policy is described to voters. “I can move it up to three-quarters [percent approval] if I talk about it being a guaranteed right to healthcare or eliminating insurance premiums and reducing out-of-pocket costs,” she said of survey respondents’ support, on a recent episode of the What the Health? From KFF Health News podcast. “I can plummet that support down to the 20s if I talk about it requiring people to pay more in taxes or threatening the current Medicare program.” What the Health? From KFF Health News A Blue Wave Hits Healthcare Episode 470 Nov. 5, 2026 The predicted blue wave in the 2026 midterms not only appeared — it overperformed, with Democrats sweeping into majorities in the House and Senate. That sets up a new focus on health policy, with Democrats seeking to undo cuts imposed by President Donald Trump and the GOP-led Congress and advance their own agenda to increase coverage and lower costs. In this special episode, host Julie Rovner is joined by Mollyann Brodie, executive vice president and chief operating officer at KFF; Larry Levitt, KFF’s executive vice president for health policy; and Amanda Seitz, Washington health policy reporter for KFF Health News. Listen Now Medicare Faces Headwinds A second problem Democrats face is that the Medicare program itself, which covers adults 65 and older and some people with disabilities, is on less-than-firm financial footing. As of this year, the trust fund that underpins the hospital insurance part of the program is projected to become insolvent in 2033 . Costs are rising for Medicare beneficiaries as well. The program requires significant out-of-pocket spending on premiums, deductibles, and coinsurance. At the same time, traditional Medicare fails to cover much-needed services such as dental, vision, hearing, and, most expensively, long-term care. Beefing up Medicare benefits would be expensive and likely require large tax increases, according to most outside estimates. The new Democratic majorities in Congress will have to decide whether their priority is to reverse the spending cuts made by the Trump administration — both to the Medicaid program for low-income and disabled people and to Affordable Care Act health plans — or to expand coverage and lower costs, turning back time to before President Donald Trump’s second term began. “Expectations are super high among voters right now, and they are demanding action on healthcare costs,” Brodie said. There are already indications that Democratic leaders are listening to the Medicare-for-All wing of their party. A day before being officially nominated as the next speaker of the House, Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York voiced support for expanding government-funded coverage, including by lowering the age of Medicare eligibility and covering all children. Of course, even if Democrats can pass legislation to restore what was cut by the GOP, there is every expectation that Trump — who has referred to Medicare for All in the past as “ a socialist takeover of our healthcare system ” — would veto those efforts. And the new majorities, while large, are not veto-proof. Finally, Democrats must face a reality that both parties often forget: The larger your majority, the more ideologically diverse it will be. While the next Congress will include more progressives pursuing Medicare for All, it will also have plenty more moderate members from swing districts currently represented by Republicans. It’s the reverse of the splits that plagued the GOP in the current Congress, with conservatives from safe red districts pitted against moderates from purplish ones. A Deeper Dissatisfaction? There is one big difference in the coming Democrat-on-Democrat debates compared with those in 1993 and 2009. One thing that has hamstrung Democrats trying to fix the health system is resistance from a plurality, if not a majority, of Americans who are relatively satisfied with their current health coverage. During the Clinton-era health reform debate, those people were represented in the famous “ Harry and Louise ” ads sponsored by the health insurance industry, featuring a couple at their kitchen table worrying that proposed changes would leave them worse off financially. KFF’s September tracking poll found instead that not only was the professed support for Medicare for All at its highest since the organization started regularly asking about it, but also a majority of respondents said they would support the policy even if it meant eliminating the private insurance industry. That’s a first, and a significant change at that. It suggests the public is so fed up with the status quo that they’d rather risk something completely new than stick with what they have. Of course, that sentiment could change fast when industry opposition revs up its counter-campaign. Still, the survey results suggest the next health reform debate could start with a public ready for something bigger. Now it’s up to the people who could make it happen to get on the same page. HealthBent, a regular feature of KFF Health News, offers insight into and analysis of policies and politics from KFF Health News chief Washington correspondent Julie Rovner, who has covered healthcare for more than 40 years.
